title: Jump High: A Job Placement Programme for the Visually Impaired
author: Charles Degold Gomez
excerpt: Jump high is a sub project under start now with the sole aim of creating job placement and internship for the visually impaired and partially sighted people in the Gambia.
content: Jump high is a sub project under start now with the sole aim of creating job placement and internship for the visually impaired and partially sighted people in the Gambia.

The project will also focus on building self-esteem of the visually impaired and partially sighted people transforming them into social visionaries and leaders in various societies and to advocate and cultivate in the mindset of the society the need for a social change towards the visually impaired and partially sighted people.

Visually impaired and partially people in the Gambia under take steps to become educated and employed. They are often seen as incompetent by the society and as a burden by the family, they could only dream of having a family and living an independent life.

Discrimination has always been a challenge for the visually impaired and partially sighted person to overcome. In the Gambia the only place to earning income for the visually impaired is the street where they can be begging and if some are fortunate to go to the college, they end up becoming classroom teacher with less paid salaries per month. The Gambia has a population of 1.8 million and 75% of the population is within the youthful age from 18 to 40. The approximated number of visually impaired and partially sighted is said to be around 45000.

Therefore, my project has come to transform the mindset of the society and to developing and building the self-esteem of the visually impaired and partially people by placing them into various qualified jobs and leadership roles  that the society never expect them to be. We want to tell the whole world that the challenges of yesterday are the opportunities of today

title: A Kanthari for Change Makers: Profiling Sabriye Tenberken
author: Charles Degold Gomez
excerpt: A Kanthari for Change Makers
content: A Kanthari for Change Makers
By Archana ravi | thiruvananthapuram
Published: 25th August 2014 06:00 AM

Last Updated: 23rd August 2014 12:55 AM
Email 16

There is a pivotal moment from which one starts to look at oneself and life differently. Sabriye Tenberken, a visually-challenged person and the Co-Founder of Kanthari (an institute to groom social entrepreneurs), calls this a “pinching point”. Her own pinching point? She says she had several. One of the earliest was when at the School for the Blind in Marburg, Germany, she told her teachers that she wanted to try out single whitewater kayaking (a sport that involves paddling in moving water). The teachers did not hesitate to say yes. She was encouraged by the trust her teachers placed in her.

Sabriye lost her eyesight when she was 12, but it is no disability, she says. “It can be a disability, say if I were to be a bus driver. But not otherwise. Normal people cannot be a sumo wrestler. So do we say they have a disability in becoming sumo wrestlers?,” she asks raising a pertinent point.

She had another pinching point while studying Sociology and Tibetology at Bonn University, Germany. She was the Student President and in a meeting when the professors unitedly backed one view, she had another opinion. When she voiced her idea, she heard a professor whisper, “First she is blind, then she has to open her mouth.” Sabriye says, “It was both saddening and uplifting at the same time. I realised then that my role in life is to be an obstacle. That I have the right to say what I felt like.”

While she was at Bonn, she travelled to Tibet and decided that’s where her mission was. She had to drop out of college, to settle down in a place where most people held the belief that the visually-challenged brought ill luck. For the blind children, who were considered as outcasts, she wanted to set up a school. She wanted to empower them. She shared the dream with her friend Paul Kronenberg, an engineer.

The school they set up in Lhasa, Tibet, named the Centre for the Blind, is today run by its first-generation students. Sabriye says that 85 per cent of the graduates from her school are self-employed. Says the 2013 INK Fellow, “Why were they successful when the odds were against them? It is because they have nothing to lose. They had freedom as they had no hold in the society. They grew up into highly reliable people who could challenge the status quo. They became a Kanthari.” Kanthari in Malayalam is the name of a variety of chilli. Kanthari, the residential programme Sabriye and Paul run in Thiruvananthapuram, is meant to mentor and shape social entrepreneurs and change makers. “The red chilli looks small and harmless, until you bite into it. Then you realise that it is spicy, but still good for health for its vitamins. At the programme, if a participant is tagged red kanthari, it means they are activists. Then there are the green kantharis, who are initiators. The yellow kantharis are inventors. The orange ones have a business mind and can be social entrepreneurs. Then there are the purple ones. Artists and writers who make a difference belong to this group,” says Sabriye.

She believes that a person who has gone through a problem and overcome it can solve others’ woes. Most of the participants have been through challenging life situations. Some of them are visually-challenged. Perhaps why, if you need to ask for directions to Kanthari, you need to ask for a school for the visually-challenged at the Vellayani Junction. “My vision is that we move away from Kanthari, and it should be run by the graduating students,” says Sabriye.

title: World White Cane Safety Day: A History
author: Charles Degold Gomez
excerpt: World White Cane Day
content: World White Cane Day

On October 15, White Cane Safety Day is observed around the world. ... White Cane Safety Day celebrates the achievements of blind or visually impaired people. A white cane is an important mobility tool for such people as well as the symbol of their independent.

Today, the white cane isn’t just a tool used by travelers with vision loss. It is a symbol for members of our community who are blind or visually impaired. White Cane Safety Day is observed annually on October 15 to recognize the many achievements of blind and visually impaired citizens and the white cane as a tool promoting independent travel.

There are references of blind travelers using a stick, cane, or shepherd’s staff as a tool for independent travel since biblical times. It has only been during the last century that the white cane has served the dual role of both a tool for travel and symbol identifying the user as a blind traveler. As early as 1921, artist James Briggs, who lost his sight in an accident, claimed to have used the first white cane as a symbol when he painted his cane white to alert passing motorists that he was a blind traveler. Ten years later, in France, Guilly d'Herbemont undertook a national "white stick" movement to promote the use of white canes. This idea spread to England when the BBC suggested in press coverage of this movement that all citizens who were blind or visually impaired be provided with a "white stick" as a universal symbol for a blind or visually impaired traveler.
In 1931, the Lion’s Clubs in North America independently began promoting the white cane for travel when one of its members observed a blind traveler at a street crossing using a black cane for mobility, which was barely visible to motorists and passers-by.

After blinded World War II veterans began returning home in greater numbers and seeking greater reintegration into their communities, Dr. Richard Hoover developed a longer white cane or "Hoover Cane" to be used both as a tool for travel as well as a symbol. In the decades prior to the Hoover Cane, the white cane was often held outright by travelers in a fixed, diagonal position.

Peoria, Illinois, was the first community to pass a special ordinance for white cane travel in 1930, which granted travelers with a white cane the right of way. Five years later, Detroit passed a similar law, later adopted by the state of Michigan. On October 6, 1964, after lobbying by various organizations, a joint resolution of Congress was enacted, which read, "Resolved by the Senate and House of Representatives that the President is hereby authorized to issue annually a proclamation designating October 15th as White Cane Safety Day and calling upon everyone to observe such a day by posting the white cane on there social media platform.

In 2000, President Clinton reminded the nation that on October 15, "With proper training, people using the white cane can enjoy greater mobility and safety by determining the location of curbs, steps, uneven pavement, and other physical obstacles in their path. The white cane has given them the freedom to travel independently to their schools and workplaces and to participate more fully in the life of their communities. It reminds us that the only barriers against people with disabilities are discriminatory attitudes and practices that our society has too often placed in their way. As we observe White Cane Safety Day, let us recall the history of the white cane, its emergence as a tool and a symbol through history; a staff of independence. Let us also recall the events that have permitted us to celebrate October 15th as White Cane Safety Day."

He received a cordial parental care especially from his mum who inspired him to be a disabled mentor. He received his primary and middle education in Kudang then proceeded to Armitage Senior Secondary School which was chosen to him by his dad. 
Lamin's intention was to be enrolled in Muslim Senior Secondary School but his Father perceived the school environment as inaccessible compared to Armitage. Lamin like many other persons with disabilities have been bullied and discriminated but his passion for education made it possible to surpass all the odd and  perceptions attached to persons with disabilities. 
He participated in many educational competitions and proven that disability is not inability. 
 Because of his fervent passion for education, he acquired higher teacher certificate at the Gambia college and later proceeded to the university where he read development studies.

content:
Today in our Disability Radio program we had the honor and privilege to host Anchar Sarr.
Anchar is a 21 year old Lady with Albinism, a second year medical student at the University of The Gambia whose dream is to specialize in dermatology.  Anchar's dreams emerge as a result of the dissatisfactory encounters she continues to receive each time she visits the skin unit at the General Hospital in Banjul.

Albinism is a genetic condition inherited from both parents, regardless of ethnicity or gender, the phenomenon remains widely misunderstood. According to data provided by the World Health Organization, estimates of its incidence vary from one in 5,000 to one in 15,000 in sub-Saharan Africa. In Tanzania, by some estimates, one in 19 people carry the genes. Collecting data on people with Albinism remains a challenge, as many with the condition are forced to hide in fear of the stigma it carries. It’s also important to realize that albinism is not a uniquely African issue but rather a global health issue. In Europe and North America, one in every 17,000 to 20,000 people also have some form of Albinism.

According to Anchar, the sun is one of the major challenges faced by Persons with Albinism which could lead to skin cancer if sun cream is not provided for proper care. 
"These sun creams are very expensive and hard to find here in the Gambia which is a concern for the Albino community" she highlighted.

title: BethGold Foundation Meets with the Mayor of Kanifing Municipal Council
author: Charles Degold Gomez
excerpt: On 16 November, the executives from the Bethgold Foundation engaged in a fruitful discussion with the Mayor of the KMC regarding a collaborative effort to improve the treatment...
content: On 16 November, the executives from the Bethgold Foundation engaged in a fruitful discussion with the Mayor of the KMC regarding a collaborative effort to improve the treatment of persons with disabilities. The meeting aimed to establish a partnership that would contribute to enhancing the lives of individuals with disabilities within the community.
Key Points Discussed:
Partnership Objectives:

Both parties expressed a shared commitment to fostering inclusivity and improving the overall well-being of persons with disabilities.
The Bethgold Foundation outlined its initiatives, emphasizing the importance of community involvement and support.
Collaborative Initiatives:

The executives presented specific projects and programs geared towards disability enhancement, including awareness campaigns, skill development workshops, and accessibility improvements in public spaces.
Media Outreach:

A notable proposal involved securing airtime on the KMC local radio for discussions on disability-related issues. This platform would serve to raise awareness, share success stories, and address challenges faced by the disabled community.
Community Involvement:

The executives and the Mayor discussed the importance of engaging the local community in these initiatives. Strategies were explored to encourage active participation and understanding of the needs of persons with disabilities.
Agreed Action Steps:
Memorandum of Understanding (MoU):

Both parties agreed to draft and finalize an MoU outlining the terms of their collaboration. This document will serve as the foundation for their joint efforts.
Radio Airtime Arrangements:

Detailed discussions took place regarding the logistics of securing regular airtime on the KMC local radio. This included content planning, scheduling, and coordination with relevant stakeholders.
Public Awareness Campaign:

Plans were set in motion for a joint public awareness campaign, utilizing various channels to inform the community about the collaborative efforts and encourage support.
Follow-up Meetings:

A commitment was made to schedule periodic follow-up meetings to assess progress, address challenges, and adapt strategies as needed.
The meeting concluded on a positive note, with both parties expressing optimism about the potential impact of their collaboration on the lives of persons with disabilities in the KMC. The Bethgold Foundation looks forward to working closely with the Mayor's office to create a more inclusive and supportive community.

title: Navigating Parenthood: Radio Discussion on Children with ADHD and Autism
author: Charles Degold Gomez
excerpt: Navigating Parenthood: Insights from Yesterday's Radio Discussion on Children with Disabilities
content: Navigating Parenthood: Insights from Yesterday's Radio Discussion on Children with Disabilities

In a thought-provoking radio discussion held yesterday 18th November at Radio Veritas102.9Fm, the spotlight was on the challenges faced by parents raising children with disabilities. The engaging program, hosted by Charles Degold Gomez , featured enlightening insights from guests Ramatoulia Bah and Umaru Fofanah, shedding light on the often misunderstood world of parenting children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and autism.

Ramatoulia Bah, a resilient mother, bravely shared her journey of raising a child with ADHD and autism. Her narrative delved into the moment she first noticed the symptoms, emphasizing the importance of recognizing early indicators. She highlighted the societal perceptions surrounding children with disabilities, recounting instances where some traditional beliefs attributed these conditions to the influence of malevolent spirits.

Umaru Fofanah, another distinguished guest on the program, brought a unique perspective to the discussion. Drawing from his own experiences working with children with disabilities, he provided valuable insights into the challenges faced by both parents and professionals in navigating the complexities of these conditions.

title: Why Persons with Disabilities Are Still Marginalized in Society
author: Charles Degold Gomez
excerpt: Why Persons with Disabilities are still marginalized and discriminated in a society?
content: Why Persons with Disabilities are still marginalized and discriminated in a society?
Persons with disabilities often face marginalization and discrimination in society due to a combination of attitudinal, institutional, and environmental factors:

1. Societal Stereotypes and Stigma:
Deep-rooted stereotypes and misconceptions about disabilities contribute to the stigmatization of individuals with disabilities. Negative attitudes and lack of understanding perpetuate discrimination.

2. Lack of Awareness and Education:
Limited awareness about various disabilities and their impact can lead to fear or discomfort. Education gaps contribute to misconceptions, hindering the acceptance and inclusion of persons with disabilities.

3. Inaccessible Infrastructure:
Physical barriers in the environment, such as inaccessible buildings and public spaces, create obstacles for individuals with disabilities. Lack of accommodations and assistive technologies further limit their participation.

4. Employment Discrimination:
Discrimination in the workplace, including prejudiced hiring practices and inadequate accommodations, can hinder career opportunities for individuals with disabilities, leading to economic marginalization.

5. Limited Legal Protections:
Weak or inadequately enforced legal frameworks for disability rights can result in insufficient protection against discrimination. Strengthening and enforcing anti-discrimination laws is crucial for promoting inclusivity.

6. Lack of Inclusive Policies:
Absence of comprehensive policies that prioritize disability inclusion may contribute to systemic exclusion. Governments and organizations need to actively implement and enforce inclusive policies.

7. Social and Economic Inequality:
Persons with disabilities often experience higher levels of poverty and limited access to resources. Socioeconomic inequalities exacerbate their vulnerability to discrimination and marginalization.

8. Communication Barriers:
Insufficient provision of accessible information and communication exacerbates the isolation of individuals with disabilities. This includes barriers in written and digital communication, as well as lack of sign language interpretation.

9. Attitudinal Barriers:
Negative attitudes and preconceived notions about the capabilities of individuals with disabilities can result in exclusion from social activities, limiting their opportunities for community engagement.

10. Underrepresentation in Decision-Making:
Limited representation of individuals with disabilities in decision-making bodies and policy development can result in oversight of their needs and perspectives.

Addressing these issues requires a holistic approach that involves changing societal attitudes, implementing and enforcing inclusive policies, improving accessibility, and promoting education and awareness about disabilities. It's a collective responsibility to create a more inclusive and equitable society for persons with disabilities.

title: International Day of Persons with Disabilities: A Position Paper to the National Assembly
author: Charles Degold Gomez
excerpt: As the world commemorates the international Day of Persons with Disabilities with the theme: United in action to rescue and achieve the SDGs for, with and by Persons with disabi...
content: As the world commemorates the international Day of Persons with Disabilities with the theme: United in action to rescue and achieve the SDGs for, with and by Persons with disabilities.
I present a position Paper on Rights and Social Inclusion of Persons with Disabilities. A call to action to our esteemed Members of the National Assembly,

I am writing to bring your attention to the imperative issue of ensuring the rights and social inclusion of persons with disabilities in our nation. Recognizing the principles of equality, diversity, and human rights, it is crucial for our legislative body to champion policies that create an inclusive society for all.
Key Points to bring to your attention:

1. Legal Protections:
Advocate for robust legislation that safeguards the rights of persons with disabilities, ensuring their equal access to education, employment, healthcare, and public services. Strengthen and enforce anti-discrimination laws to protect against any form of disability-based prejudice.

2. Inclusive Education:
Support initiatives that promote inclusive education, providing accessible learning environments and accommodations. Encourage the integration of disability awareness and sensitivity training into educational curricula to foster understanding and acceptance.

3. Employment Opportunities:
Advocate for policies that encourage businesses to implement inclusive hiring practices, providing reasonable accommodations for employees with disabilities. Incentivize companies to create accessible workplaces, promoting diversity and equal opportunities.

4. Accessible Infrastructure:
Prioritize the development of universally accessible infrastructure, including public transportation, buildings, and digital platforms. Ensure that urban planning considers the needs of persons with disabilities to create barrier-free environments.

5. Social Welfare Programs:
Strengthen social welfare programs to address the specific needs of individuals with disabilities. Ensure that disability benefits are sufficient to cover healthcare, assistive technologies, and support services that enable independent living.

6. Community Engagement:
Encourage community initiatives that foster social inclusion and break down stereotypes. Support organizations that promote recreational activities, cultural events, and social opportunities for individuals with disabilities to actively participate in community life.

7. Accessible Information and Communication:
Advocate for the creation and enforcement of standards for accessible information and communication, including websites, documents, and public announcements. Ensure that communication methods are inclusive and cater to diverse needs.

8. Healthcare Accessibility:
Prioritize accessible healthcare services and facilities for persons with disabilities. Advocate for comprehensive healthcare coverage, including rehabilitation services, mental health support, and specialized care.

In conclusion, as representatives of the people, we have the responsibility to champion the rights and social inclusion of persons with disabilities. By advocating for inclusive policies, we contribute to a society where every individual, regardless of ability, can live a dignified and fulfilling life. Let us work together to create a nation that values and embraces the diversity of its citizens.
Thank you for your attention and dedication to the well-being of all members of our society.

Sincerely,

As word of Alieu's initiative spread, the program gained recognition and support. Blind individuals who once felt limited by societal expectations found themselves equipped with the tools to navigate the digital landscape independently.

Jaiteh's resilience faced a defining moment when funding dwindled, threatening the continuity of his program. Undaunted, he leveraged social media and community outreach, rallying support from local businesses and individuals and  organizations. The response was overwhelming, demonstrating the collective belief in the transformative impact of Jaiteh's work.

Ultimately, Alieu's story became a testament to the resilience of the human spirit. Through his computer literacy program, he not only empowered blind individuals with valuable skills but also shattered misconceptions about their capabilities. title: Wings of Knowledge: Lamin K. Fatty's Journey Beyond Disability Stereotypes
author: Charles Degold Gomez
excerpt: "Wings of Knowledge: Breaking Free from Disability Stereotypes.
content: "Wings of Knowledge: Breaking Free from Disability Stereotypes.

In a small village from the western part of Africa, there lived a boy named Lamin K Fatty  who faced not only the challenges of a physical disability but also the heavy burden of societal prejudice. Born with a condition that affected his mobility, Lamin confronted a world that often saw him through a lens of pity and discrimination.

As Lamin entered the local school, he was met with whispered remarks and condescending glances from both students and even some educators. The physical barriers of the school compounded his struggles, making it challenging for him to navigate the classrooms and hallways.

Despite his genuine enthusiasm for learning, Lamin Fatty found himself isolated, the target of cruel taunts and exclusion from group activities. The stigma surrounding his disability became a heavy weight on his shoulders, casting a shadow over his academic journey.

Teachers, instead of offering support, sometimes underestimated Lamin's abilities, inadvertently reinforcing the prejudiced beliefs held by some of his classmates. The once bright spark in Lamin's eyes began to dim as he internalized the harsh judgments imposed upon him.

The school's administration, although aware of the situation, failed to address the pervasive stigma. Lamin's pleas for understanding and acceptance fell on deaf ears, leaving him trapped in a cycle of loneliness and despair.

Despite the adversity, Lamin Fatty clung to his dreams of education being the pathway to a better future. With sheer determination, he sought solace in books and self-study, finding refuge in the world of knowledge when the social world rejected him.

A turning point came when a compassionate teacher recognized Lamin's potential and advocated for his inclusion in various school activities. Slowly, a few classmates began to challenge their preconceived notions, and a subtle shift in attitudes started to occur.

While the scars of prejudice remained, Lamin's resilience allowed him to graduate with honors. His story, though painful, became a catalyst for change in the community, forcing reflection on the damaging impact of societal biases. Lamin's journey highlights the urgent need for education systems to not only provide academic knowledge but also actively challenge and dismantle the prejudices that hinder the growth and potential of every child, regardless of their abilities.

Lamin in his quest for an inclusive society, is honoured with a Maters scholarship to study Pulic policy focusing on social policy in the US. In a new environment that embraces disability inclusion and diversity , his vision is make the Gambia an inclusive society that embraces inclusivity.

title: A Call for Inclusive Action: Recognizing the Deaf Community in The Gambia
author: Charles Degold Gomez
excerpt: "A Call for Inclusive Action: Recognizing the Rights and Potential of the Deaf Community in The Gambia"
content: "A Call for Inclusive Action: Recognizing the Rights and Potential of the Deaf Community in The Gambia"

The UN General Assembly has proclaimed 23 September as the International Day of Sign Languages in order to raise awareness of the importance of sign language in the full realization of the human rights of people who are deaf.

As we mark Deaf Awareness Month, we stand united with the Deaf community in The Gambia, urging our leaders and policymakers to take immediate and meaningful action. Deaf individuals deserve equal access to education, healthcare, employment, and public services, as enshrined in both national and international human rights frameworks.
We call upon the Government to:
1. Strengthen the legal framework protecting the rights of Deaf individuals, ensuring full implementation of the Disability Rights Act.

2. Invest in education by supporting the training of more sign language interpreters, making sign language education mandatory in schools, and providing accessible learning environments for Deaf students.
3. Promote Deaf employment by ensuring that workplaces are inclusive, and that Deaf individuals have access to training and employment opportunities.
4. Raise public awareness on the importance of sign language and Deaf culture to foster a more inclusive society where Deaf people can thrive without barriers.

The Deaf community has the potential to contribute immensely to the development of The Gambia, but this can only happen if their rights are respected and their voices—spoken through sign language—are heard. It’s time to make The Gambia a leader in inclusion, where no one is left behind.

title: The Gambia's Disability Inclusion Gap — And the African Models We Can Adopt
author: Charles Degold Gomez
excerpt: The Gambia’s Disability Inclusion Gap — And the African Models We Can Adopt Today.
content: The Gambia’s Disability Inclusion Gap — And the African Models We Can Adopt Today.

"People often underestimate our abilities. Employers become reluctant and tell us they cannot give jobs to people like us, and taxi drivers will often refuse to pick us up, claiming we are too slow."
— Adama Jallow, a Persons Living with Disabilities
In The Gambia, over 10% of the population lives with a disability. Yet many face double discrimination based on both gender and disability limiting access to education, employment, and leadership.

The challenges are systemic:
1. Economic exclusion: Denied employment and transport access despite relying on trade for livelihoods.
2. Political invisibility: Persons with disabilities are often excluded from public decision-making processes that affect their lives.
3. Implementation gap: The Gambia passed the Persons with Disability Act in July 2021, but progress on the ground remains slow.
We don’t need to reinvent the wheel. Africa already has the blueprint.
5. Proven Models The Gambia Can Adapt:

1. Political Representation – Uganda, Kenya, Rwanda, Zimbabwe, Egypt. 
These 5 countries constitutionally guarantee parliamentary seats for persons with disabilities. Representation shifts PWDs from beneficiaries to decision-makers.

2. Inclusive Employment – Zambia & Kenya.
Tax incentives for employers hiring 10+ persons with disabilities, plus mandates for workplace modifications. Zambia and Kenya are leading here.

3. Accessible Infrastructure – Senegal. 
Dakar’s Bus Rapid Transit was designed with ramp access, retrofitted sidewalks, and accessible stations for PWDs from day one.
4. TVET & Skills – South Africa.
Technical and Vocational Education Training colleges are addressing barriers related to disability, gender, and socio-economic status to boost employability.
5. Government Ownership – Cross-Country Evidence.
Projects succeed when "owned by government and local authorities" because they hold the power to scale and sustain impact.

The Path Forward for The Gambia:
The 2021 Act is a foundation. Now we need:
- Reserved seats in local councils and National Assembly.
- Tax breaks + "Access to Work" grants for PWD entrepreneurs
- Mandatory accessibility in all new infrastructure projects
- Nationwide media training to dismantle stigma
Disability inclusion isn’t charity. It’s economic sense, human rights, and good governance.
To my network in policy, development, and private sector: Which of these models should The Gambia prioritize in 2026? And how can we partner to move from legislation to implementation?

Let’s connect if you’re working on inclusive policy or employment in West Africa.

title: The Power of Family Support: A Disability Radio Conversation with Ebrima Sarr
author: Charles Degold Gomez
excerpt: 🎙️ IN EVERY DISABILITY, THERE IS ABILITY – THE POWER OF FAMILY SUPPORT
content: 🎙️ IN EVERY DISABILITY, THERE IS ABILITY – THE POWER OF FAMILY SUPPORT

BethGold Foundation, in partnership with Radio Veritas 102.9FM, hosted another impactful Disability Radio Talk Show, creating a platform for voices that inspire, educate, and challenge society's perceptions about disability.
We were honored to welcome Mr. Ebrima Sarr, Founder and President of the Young Disability Foundation in Fass Njagga Choi, Lower Nuimi District, North Bank Region.
Ebrima shared his remarkable journey of growing up as a child with a disability and how the unwavering love and support of his family shaped the person and leader he is today.
One statement that deeply resonated with everyone listening was:

"My family supported me so much because they believed in me. And that is why I am encouraging all families to support their children with disabilities. Charity begins at home. Before anyone supports you, it has to start from home first."

Those words remind us that the first place where inclusion begins is not in government offices, schools, or workplaces—it begins at home. When families choose love over stigma, encouragement over pity, and opportunity over limitation, children with disabilities are empowered to dream, lead, and transform their communities.
Today, Ebrima is living proof of that truth.

Through the Young Disability Foundation, with the support of Activista The Gambia  and the Gambia Ports Authority, he is now giving back by empowering persons with disabilities across the North Bank Region and beyond. His story is a powerful reminder that when we invest in one person, that person can go on to impact hundreds of others.
At BethGold Foundation, we remain committed to amplifying these stories, promoting disability inclusion, and advocating for equal opportunities for every person with a disability.
Together, we can build a society where disability is never seen as inability, but as part of the rich diversity of humanity.
Let us all remember: Believe in a child with a disability. Support them. Encourage them. Empower them. The journey to an inclusive society starts at home.

title: Creating Awareness Through Sickle Cell Education
author: Charles Degold Gomez
excerpt: 🩸 Creating Awareness Through Sickle Cell Education
content: 🩸 Creating Awareness Through Sickle Cell Education

BethGold Foundation  was honored to host the Sickle Cell Association – The Gambia on our Disability Radio Talk Show on Radio Veritas 102.9FM, as part of our commitment to raising awareness on disability, health, and inclusion.

Our guest Musa Dem (President) and Gabriel Jawneh (Secretary), courageously shared their personal journeys as individuals living with sickle cell disease. They spoke openly about the daily battles they face—the excruciating pain crises, the silent struggles that often go unseen, and the resilience it takes to keep moving forward despite the challenges.

The discussion also provided an important opportunity to educate listeners about Sickle Cell Disease, its causes, the myths surrounding it, and the importance of early awareness. One of the key messages emphasized during the program was the need for genotype testing before marriage. Knowing your genotype empowers couples to make informed decisions, helping to reduce the number of children born with sickle cell disease.

At BethGold Foundation, we believe that awareness saves lives, education empowers communities, and prevention begins with knowledge. Together, we can break the stigma, support those living with sickle cell disease, and build a healthier and more informed society.
We extend our sincere appreciation to the Sickle Cell Association – The Gambia, Musa Dem, and Gabriel for sharing their inspiring stories and valuable insights.
Know your genotype. Get tested. Make informed choices. Together, we can create a future with greater awareness, compassion, and hope.
